disease.name: Gastroenteritis

overview.description: Gastroenteritis is an inflammation of the mucous membrane lining the stomach and small intestine, commonly known as 'stomach flu' (though unrelated to influenza). It leads to diarrhea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and dehydration. Most cases are viral and self-limiting, but bacterial and parasitic forms can be more severe.
overview.prevalence: Extremely common; estimated 1.5–2 billion cases worldwide annually, major cause of childhood mortality in developing countries.
overview.age_group: All ages; highest severity in infants, young children, elderly, and immunocompromised individuals

types.name: Viral Gastroenteritis
types.description: Most common type caused by norovirus, rotavirus, adenovirus, or astrovirus. Highly contagious and usually self-resolving.
types.common_in: Children, schools, cruise ships, and households

types.name: Bacterial Gastroenteritis
types.description: Caused by bacteria such as Salmonella, Campylobacter, Shigella, E. coli (ETEC, EHEC), or Vibrio. Often linked to food poisoning.
types.common_in: Travelers, areas with poor hygiene, undercooked meat/eggs

types.name: Parasitic Gastroenteritis
types.description: Caused by parasites like Giardia lamblia, Cryptosporidium, or Entamoeba histolytica.
types.common_in: Contaminated water sources, travelers to endemic areas

types.name: Traveler's Diarrhea
types.description: Acute gastroenteritis occurring during or shortly after travel, often bacterial.

severity_levels.name: Mild
severity_levels.frequency: Few loose stools, mild nausea, no significant dehydration
severity_levels.impact: Managed at home with oral rehydration and rest

severity_levels.name: Moderate
severity_levels.frequency: Frequent diarrhea/vomiting, low-grade fever, mild dehydration
severity_levels.impact: Requires close monitoring and ORS; medical consultation advised

severity_levels.name: Severe
severity_levels.frequency: Profuse diarrhea/vomiting, high fever, moderate to severe dehydration
severity_levels.impact: Requires medical intervention, possible hospitalization and IV fluids

genetic_factors: Lack of FUT2 gene (natural resistance to norovirus in some individuals)
environmental_triggers: Consumption of contaminated food or water
other_causes: Medication side effects (antibiotics causing C. difficile)
Toxins from certain bacteria (Staphylococcus aureus, Bacillus cereus)

primary_symptoms.name: Watery Diarrhea
primary_symptoms.description: Frequent loose or watery stools, sometimes explosive.

primary_symptoms.name: Nausea and Vomiting
primary_symptoms.description: Feeling of sickness with repeated vomiting.

primary_symptoms.name: Abdominal Cramps
primary_symptoms.description: Painful cramping or bloating in the stomach and intestines.

warning_signs_of_attack: Signs of severe dehydration (sunken eyes, dry mouth, reduced urine output)
Severe abdominal pain (possible appendicitis or other complications)
Persistent vomiting preventing any fluid intake

medical_history: Recent travel, food consumption history, contact with sick individuals
Assessment of fluid intake and urine output
physical_examination: Vital signs (heart rate, blood pressure, temperature)
Skin turgor and mucous membrane moisture

diagnostic_tests.purpose: Identify causative virus, bacteria, or parasite

diagnostic_tests.description: Measures sodium, potassium, and signs of infection.
Quick stool test for common viruses.

medicines.note: All medications should be taken only under the supervision of a licensed physician. Self-medication can be dangerous.

categories.purpose: Replace fluids and electrolytes lost due to diarrhea and vomiting

medicines.name: Oral Rehydration Salts (ORS)
medicines.dosage: After every loose stool as per WHO guidelines

medicines.name: Ciprofloxacin
medicines.use_case: Certain bacterial cases (not E. coli O157)

medicines.name: Loperamide
medicines.dosage: 4 mg initially, then 2 mg after each loose stool

diet_and_nutrition.overview: Diet focuses on gentle, easily digestible foods while prioritizing hydration to support gut recovery.

items.benefit: Binding effect reduces diarrhea; potassium restoration
Easy to digest and restores gut flora

foods_to_avoid.reason: Temporary lactose intolerance common after gastroenteritis

sample_meal_plan.note: Start with clear liquids, progress slowly. Consult doctor if severe.
sample_meal_plan.lunch: Boiled rice + mashed potato + yogurt (if tolerated)

special_dietary_notes: Gradually reintroduce normal diet after 24-48 hours of improvement

trigger_avoidance: Avoid close contact with infected individuals
hydration: Sip ORS or homemade sugar-salt solution frequently
Monitor urine output (should be pale yellow)

complications.description: Rare complication of E. coli infection leading to kidney failure.
Especially in prolonged or recurrent cases.

key_points: Leading cause of childhood hospitalization in developing countries
Rotavirus vaccine highly effective for prevention
Higher risk of severe dehydration and complications

vaccinations_recommended.reason: Prevents severe viral gastroenteritis in infants

when_to_see_doctor: Blood in stool or black stools
High fever or severe abdominal pain
emergency_signs: Severe dehydration (no urine for 8+ hours, sunken eyes)
Shock (cold clammy skin, rapid weak pulse)

frequently_asked_questions.question: How long does gastroenteritis last?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Viral cases usually resolve in 1-3 days for adults and 3-7 days for children. Bacterial cases may last longer.

frequently_asked_questions.question: When should antibiotics be used?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Only for confirmed bacterial infections. Most cases are viral and do not require antibiotics.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Can I take anti-diarrheal medicine?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Generally avoided in children and in cases with fever or bloody diarrhea as it can prolong infection.

references: WHO Guidelines on Acute Diarrhea Management
UpToDate: Acute Viral Gastroenteritis in Adults and Children
